title: The company of great souls
hook: a servant's boy among singing sages, and the sutras' chief means of love
carry: love of God is caught in satsang

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti and the king and the meal: knowing about a meal doesn't end your hunger, and love is its own fruit.
screen: `THE KING AND THE MEAL.` · `ITS OWN FRUIT.`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata Purana, Narada tells how he began. In an earlier life, he says, he was the small son of a maidservant. One rainy season a group of sages came to stay where his mother worked, and the boy was set to serve them. He fetched water, kept quiet, ate what they left with their permission, and every day heard them singing and telling the stories of Krishna. No study, no vow. And a taste for Krishna woke up in him, growing with every hearing. Today the sutras credited to that same Narada list how love begins, and name the one means they call chief.
screen: `A SERVANT'S BOY.` → `ONE RAINY SEASON WITH THE SAGES.` → `LOVE WAKES UP.`

segments.voice: The teachers sing of its means, the sutras say, and list them. Letting go of the pull of sense objects, and of clinging attachment. Worship that doesn't break off. Hearing and singing the qualities of the Lord, even while living an ordinary life in the world. So the means aren't only for a monastery. Then the sutras turn. But chiefly, love comes by the grace of great souls, or by a drop of the Lord's own grace. After the list of things a person can do, the main source is something given. Then three phrases about the company of the great, mahat-sanga. It is hard to find. It is hard to fathom. And in the sutras' view, it never fails. Then a line that holds the section together. Between him and his people, there is no difference. To be near those who love God, in this text, is already to be near God. And the section ends with a sentence said twice, like a teacher tapping the table: strive for that alone, strive for that alone. Narada's own beginning is this teaching lived out. It's why Hindus prize satsang, the company of the true: the bhajan circle, the temple hall, a grandmother who brings you along. In the sutras' picture, love of God travels from those who have it to whoever sits near.
screen: `LET GO, WORSHIP, HEAR AND SING.` · `CHIEFLY: THE GRACE OF GREAT SOULS.` · `NO DIFFERENCE: HIM AND HIS PEOPLE.` · `SATSANG: HOW NARADA BEGAN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a song, a chant or a name others once sang around you, at a temple, at home, in a car with the radio on, and let it play quietly inside without moving your lips. Listen the way you'd listen in a room full of people singing it together, and when the mind wanders, come back to the next line. If you pray, you can let it be a song of praise to God.
Bhakti. In the sutras it's helped along by letting go, by worship, by hearing and singing, and chiefly by the company of great souls, mahat-sanga.
Your line: love of God is caught in satsang. Love travels from the one who has it to the one sitting near. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: In devotional Hindu communities, people gather for satsang, sitting with teachers and fellow devotees to hear and sing about God, and the Narada Bhakti Sutras' lines on the company of great souls are a familiar reason given for it.

Narada Bhakti Sutras.meaning: a short book on love of God, attributed to Narada

sources.ref: Narada Bhakti Sutras 34–42 (the means: letting go of objects and attachment, unbroken worship, hearing and singing; chiefly the grace of great souls; the company of the great; no difference between him and his people; strive for that alone)
Bhagavata Purana 1.5.23–26 (Narada's past life: a maidservant's son who served sages through the rainy season and heard them sing of Krishna), as told on days 138 and 693

notes: Sutras 34–42 paraphrased. The explanations of 'hard to find, hard to fathom, never fails' are the script's gloss, not the text; confirm they are within the range of the commentaries.
Sutra 41 (tasmiṃs taj-jane bhedābhāvāt) rendered 'between him and his people there is no difference'; confirm.
'Love of God can travel the same way' is framed as the sutras' picture, not a claim about people in general; confirm it reads that way.
howItsDone names satsang; the link to these sutras is given as 'a familiar reason', not a claim about all communities.
